title: The Ten Commandments
summary: God speaks the Ten Commandments to all Israel, beginning with who he is and what he has done: the LORD who brought them out of the house of slavery. The commands forbid other gods, idols, and the misuse of his name, set apart the Sabbath, and protect parents, life, marriage, property, truth, and the neighbor from our desires. Terrified by the thunder and smoke, the people ask Moses to speak to them instead, and God gives the first laws of worship: no gods of silver or gold, and a plain altar of earth or uncut stone.
story: Chapter 19 ended with God descending on Sinai; chapter 20 is what he says. These are the only words in the book that God speaks directly to the whole people. Everything else in the law comes through Moses, at the people's own request (verse 19). The commandments open the long section of law that continues in the Book of the Covenant (20:22-23:33), which is sealed in the covenant ceremony of chapter 24. Moses will later shatter the first tablets when Israel worships the golden calf (chapter 32) and receive new ones (chapter 34), and Deuteronomy 5 repeats the commandments to the next generation on the edge of the land. From here on they are the heart of Israel's covenant, the words kept inside the ark itself.
historical:
Law collections were known in the ancient Near East long before Israel. The laws of Ur-Nammu from Sumer (around 2100 BC) and the Code of Hammurabi of Babylon (about 1750 BC) are the best known, and chapters 21-23 share many of their concerns. The Ten Commandments are different in kind. Most ancient law is case law (if someone does this, then that follows), while the commandments are unconditional statements with no penalties attached, addressed to each Israelite as you. The German scholar Albrecht Alt called this form apodictic law and argued that it was distinctive of Israel, though similar unconditional commands have since been found elsewhere.

In the 1950s George Mendenhall compared the Sinai covenant with Hittite treaties of the late second millennium BC, in which a great king names himself, recounts his past kindness to a subject people, and then lays down obligations. Verse 2 fits that pattern closely: a name, a history of rescue, then the demands. Others have compared the covenant form, especially in Deuteronomy, with Assyrian treaties of the seventh century BC. The comparison does not settle the date, but it shows that the commandments are the terms of a relationship with a king who has already acted.
cultural:
Several commandments cut against what was normal in Israel's world. Every neighboring people made images of its gods, and an image was not a mere picture. In Mesopotamia a ritual of washing the mouth was performed to bring a god's presence into a new statue, which was then clothed, fed, and carried in procession. Forbidding images meant that Israel's God could not be located, handled, or managed. The command about taking the LORD's name in vain concerns more than careless speech. Names were invoked in oaths, curses, and magic, and the Hebrew speaks of lifting up the name for emptiness: using God's name to back a false oath or to bend him to one's will.

The Sabbath had no real parallel. Babylonian calendars treated certain days of the month as unlucky, but a weekly day of rest extended to slaves, livestock, and resident foreigners appears in Israel alone. In a world where most people worked without pause, a law giving slaves a day off by divine command was startling. The honor due to parents meant, for adults, provision and respect in old age, not only obedience in childhood. And the last commandment reaches past acts to desire, which no human court can enforce.
literary: The Bible never numbers these commands; it calls them the ten words (34:28; Deuteronomy 4:13), and traditions divide them differently. Jewish tradition counts verse 2 as the first word and joins other gods and images as the second. Catholics and Lutherans, following Augustine, join other gods and images as the first commandment and divide coveting into two. Orthodox and Reformed Christians, following the older division found in Philo and Josephus, count other gods and images separately. The commands fall into two groups, toward God and toward neighbor. The first group carries reasons (verses 5-6, 7, 11), while most of the second are bare prohibitions, three of them only two words long in Hebrew. The Sabbath command rests here on creation and in Deuteronomy 5:15 on the exodus. After the commands the narrative returns to the people's fear, and then the Book of the Covenant opens, like the Decalogue itself, with God, idols, and the altar.

outline.t: The LORD who brought Israel out of slavery
No other gods and no idols
Parents, life, marriage, property, truth, and desire
The people's fear and Moses the mediator
First laws of worship: no idols and a simple altar

doctrines.note: The commandments come after the rescue, and verse 2 grounds them in it. They describe the life of a people who belong to the God who freed them, guarding his honor and the neighbor's life, marriage, property, and name. The law is a gift given to the redeemed, not a ladder climbed to earn redemption.

The first two commands forbid worshiping any other god and making any image to worship. The first guards God's uniqueness; the second keeps him from being shrunk to something people can make and manage. Verse 23 repeats the warning at once, and chapter 32 shows how quickly it is broken.

God names himself by what he has done in history, and he calls himself jealous, a word for the rightful zeal of a husband for his marriage rather than petty envy. His punishment reaches three or four generations, but his loving devotion reaches a thousand.

words.note: Qanna, jealous, used in the Bible only of God. It describes the passion of one who will not share what rightly belongs to him. It is not insecurity or spite but covenant love that refuses rivals. Exodus 34:14 goes further: “the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.”

Chesed, loving devotion, steadfast love, or covenant faithfulness: loyalty that goes beyond what is owed. The Hebrew of verse 6 says to thousands, which many translations take as a thousand generations. Either way the imbalance is deliberate. Judgment reaches three or four generations of those who hate God; chesed reaches thousands of those who love him.

Ratsach, to kill a person. The verb is used overwhelmingly for unlawful killing, including accidental manslaughter (Numbers 35), and almost never for killing in battle, which is why most modern translations render the command You shall not murder. It protects human life because people bear God's image (Genesis 9:6). Christians have differed over how the command bears on war and capital punishment.

christ: Jesus did not set these commands aside. In the Sermon on the Mount he presses them to the heart, treating contempt as a breach of the command against murder and lust as a breach of the command against adultery (Matthew 5:21-30), which is where the tenth commandment was already pointing. Asked for the greatest commandment, he answered with love for God with all one's heart, soul, and mind, and love for one's neighbor as oneself (Matthew 22:37-40), the two tables of this chapter. Paul says the commandments are summed up in “Love your neighbor as yourself” (Romans 13:9), and admits that the tenth commandment exposed his own sin (Romans 7:7). The people's plea for someone to stand between them and God's voice (verse 19) finds its New Testament answer in “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).

hard.q: Does God punish children for their parents' sins?
hard.a: Verse 5 says God visits the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generations, yet Deuteronomy 24:16 forbids putting children to death for their fathers, and Ezekiel says plainly, “The soul who sins is the one who will die” (Ezekiel 18:20). Several responses are given. Many interpreters stress the qualifying phrase, “of those who hate Me”: the punishment falls on descendants who carry on their parents' rebellion, not on innocent children. Others note that three or four generations was the span of a household living together in the ancient world, so the verse describes how one generation's idolatry damages everyone under its roof, a pattern visible in families still. Others read Ezekiel as correcting exiles who used this principle to blame their ancestors instead of repenting. On every reading the verse is lopsided by design, with judgment reaching a few generations and loving devotion reaching a thousand.

questions: The commandments begin with what God has done before they say what Israel must do. How would it change your obedience to see it as a response to rescue rather than a way to earn favor?
The tenth commandment reaches past actions to desire. Which of the other commandments do you think is usually broken first in the heart?
The Sabbath gave rest even to slaves, animals, and foreigners. What would it look like for your rest to protect the rest of other people?
